newsitem.title: ITALY: Bologna gets higher debt rating than Italy.
newsitem.headline: Bologna gets higher debt rating than Italy.

text.p: Bologna city council, which will make a first issue of some 15 billion lire worth of municipal bonds on the domestic market early in September, on Tuesday got a higher debt rating than Italy.
The issue of Buoni Ordinari Comunali (BOC) is the first tranche of a three-year medium-term (15-year) note programme for a total value equal to 120 billion lire.
Several Italian cities have already made BOC issues.
Earlier on Tuesday, Moody's Investors Service assigned a Aa2 rating to the Italian city's lira-denominated notes.
Moody's only rates the Republic of Italy's domestic and foreign debt at Aa3, the same as Portugal, Sweden and Taiwan.
With its Aa2, Bologna is on the same Moody's rating level as Australia, Canada and Spain.
Bologna's budget councillor Flavio Delbono told a news conference that Bologna "is the first European city to obtain a rating higher than the country it belongs to."
Moody's said the rating reflected Bologna's strong economy and stable political climate, as well as its solid track record of prudent fiscal management and financial flexibility.
It also took account of the current trend in Italy towards shifting budgetary responsibilities from central to regional and local government.
The only other Italian city to which Moody's has given a rating is Naples which got an Aa3, the same as Italy's.
Debt market sources familiar with ratings procedure said the fact Bologna got a higher rating than Italy was not an anomaly and did not set a precedent.
They said most sovereign domestic ratings in Western Europe were "triple As" and in principle it was difficult for a local authority to be rated above its country.

"But the Republic of Italy has been a bit of a laggard in respect of its Aa3 rating," said one source who declined to be named. However, the source noted that the Aa3 rating was not a ceiling. "The ceiling is triple A in Italy."

The sources said that in Canada there were half a dozen or so federal states or municipalities rated triple A, above Canada's Aa2 sovereign domestic debt rating, "so this rating does not set a precedent."
"Where the issuer has sufficient strength and independence, then the ratings agencies have no problem with rating a sub-sovereign at a level higher than a sovereign.

"In the case of Bologna, the city's economy and financial management is in many ways better than on a national level, its debt is at moderate levels for a European local authority and it has a good and well-deserved reputation for controlling capital expenditure. So the rating is not a surprise," the source added.
